title: Dependency Map
notes: Frame the chapter as a conversion pipeline: a moving loop becomes a class, classes multiply, maps act on classes, and calculations become obstructions. The dependency map is useful because later applications only use a few arrows, especially circle degree and functoriality.

title: Homotopy Rel Endpoints
notes: Emphasize that the square is the actual object, not a metaphor. Each horizontal slice is a based loop, while both vertical edges are pinned at the basepoint. This is what makes deformation compatible with loop multiplication later.

title: Circle Loop Deformation
notes: Use the figure to separate raw path shape from the integer endpoint of a lift. The alpha loop visibly contains a forward, forward, backward itinerary, but after homotopy rel endpoints it carries the same degree as the simpler beta loop.

title: Loop Classes Form A Group
notes: The raw concatenation operation remembers the clock, so it is too strict. Passing to homotopy classes hides harmless reparameterizations and backtracking. The checks in the notebook confirm the three group-law claims with reduced loop words.

title: Basepoints And Induced Maps
notes: Make the basepoint issue explicit before using functoriality. Moving the basepoint along a path conjugates loops, while a continuous map composes with loops and gives a homomorphism. The degree-map checks verify that induced maps compose as expected.

title: Circle Calculation
notes: This is the model calculation for the whole chapter. The covering line turns a loop problem into an endpoint problem, and the endpoint integer is the degree. The sanity data reports lift endpoint two and winding number two for the plotted loop.

title: Covering Lab
notes: Treat the lab as a place to test the path-lifting lemma rather than as a black-box animation. Students should vary a loop, watch the lift move through adjacent intervals, and check that ending over an integer records the circle class.

title: Calculation Ledger
notes: The ledger is not claiming to solve every group presentation. It records the abelian shadow that should be preserved by the examples in this chapter. Smith normal form catches mistakes such as a missing exponent in the Klein bottle or lens-space relation.

title: Orbit Spaces And Torus
notes: Connect the circle calculation to quotients by properly discontinuous actions. The torus comes from a Z by Z action on the plane, so its two generating loops are inherited from translations. The linked model and polygon image give two views of the same generators.

title: Wedge And Free Group
notes: A wedge of circles has generators but no surface relation yet. That is why the Cayley fragment branches like reduced words instead of closing into a lattice. The notebook check reports seventeen nodes in the radius-two fragment and idempotent free reduction.

title: Homotopy Type
notes: Now the invariant is no longer restricted to homeomorphism. A deformation retraction gives a concrete homotopy equivalence, so the annulus, cylinder core, and punctured plane inherit the circle group. The visual shows points flowing toward the retained core.

title: Contractible Caveats
notes: Use this slide to slow down a common overreach. Contractible implies simply connected, but the homotopy need not keep a chosen point fixed throughout. The comb-style schematic represents how a space can shrink globally while resisting a basepoint-relative contraction.

title: Brouwer Obstruction
notes: The fixed-point theorem is presented through the retraction it would force. If a fixed-point-free disc map existed, rays from f(x) through x would retract the disc to its boundary. Functoriality then asks a trivial group to surject onto Z, which is impossible.

title: Plane Separation
notes: The separation statements are not proved by the sampled grid, but the computation mirrors the theorem's contrast. A closed curve sample has two complement components, while an arc sample has one. The fundamental group enters through punctured-plane and no-retraction arguments.

title: Surface Boundary
notes: The boundary theorem uses the same obstruction pattern locally. If a point were both boundary and interior, a punctured half-disc would retract onto a circle. The punctured half-disc is contractible, so its trivial fundamental group cannot map onto the circle group.

title: Applied Recap
notes: Close by reading one loop word through several spaces. Free reduction, circle degree, torus abelianization, and the Klein parity marker are different invariants of the same symbolic input. The lab table keeps the chapter's computations inspectable and falsifiable.
